summary: Same one-shot sunrise animation with pixel-exact geometry, timing and lifecycle, but the port's warm phase is orange (255,68,0) where the original's is red (255,30,0) — a systematic ~2.3x green-channel excess that also makes the whitening transition amber instead of salmon.
observations: Both sides render, no compile or runtime errors, no controls on either side (probe: 'no settable controls' for orig AND port — control surfaces match).

Shape (both sides, 60 px strip): a warm glow is born at the strip centre and expands symmetrically outward at ~20 px/s. Lit span (orig): t=0.2 [26,34], t=0.6 [18,42], t=1.0 [10,50], t=1.4 [2,58], full strip by t=1.6. Port is identical to within 1 px at every one of those times ([27,33], [19,41], [11,49], [3,57]).

Lifecycle is a ONE-SHOT ramp, not a loop: black -> expanding warm wedge (0-1.6 s) -> a red/orange saturation front expanding from centre at ~20 px/s (orig R=255 span t=1.8 [23,37], t=2.2 [15,45], t=2.6 [7,53], whole strip by t=3.0; port trails by 1-2 px) -> ~0.4 s hold at the plateau colour -> a white front expanding from centre at ~20 px/s (orig white span t=4.6 [27,33], t=5.0 [19,41], t=5.4 [11,49], t=5.8 [3,57]; port [29,32], [21,40], [13,48], [5,56]) -> full white from ~t=6.2 onward, forever. Confirmed over a 500 s / 2 fps survey: no reset, no repeat, no second event on either side.

COLOUR, phase 1 (headline difference). Binned R->G over all pixels/times while R<255: orig G = 0.118*R (plateau 255,30,0, hue ~7 deg, fire-engine red); port G = 0.267*R (plateau 255,68,0, hue ~16 deg, vermillion/safety orange). The multiplier is constant over the whole ramp: orig R=64->G=8, 128->15, 192->23, 240->28; port R=64->G=17, 128->35, 192->51, 240->65. Plainly visible side-by-side in the waterfalls: the original's mid-window band is pure red, the port's is orange.

COLOUR, phase 2. Once R is railed at 255 the blue channel follows green with an offset, and the port's offset is much larger: orig B starts rising at G~32 and holds G-B ~27 falling to 0 (G=64->B=38, 128->111, 192->183, 240->236); port B starts rising only at G~64 and holds G-B ~50 (G=96->B=38, 128->81, 192->169, 240->233). So the original whitens through salmon/pink and the port whitens through amber/peach. Both converge on pure white.
Aggregate effect on the 6 s baseline: meanR 192.3 (orig) vs 190.1 (port), meanB 64.8 vs 62.6 — essentially equal — while meanG is 79.9 vs 96.6, +21% on the port. The whole divergence lives in green.

TIMING: brightness envelopes are near-identical. Orig meanBrightness at 0/1/2/3/4/5 s = 0/23/76/95/134/223; port = 0/24/84/108/140/222. The port lags by a constant ~0.05-0.10 s (1-2 frames at 20 fps), visible as its fronts trailing the original's by 1-2 px throughout. Nothing a viewer could see.

FRAME-RATE COUPLING (mild, and it is the ORIGINAL that is coupled): the port is byte-identical at 10, 20 and 40 fps when dumped at the same absolute times (t=1 p15 = 255-scale 42,11,0 at all three rates; t=4 p15 = 255,99,42 at all three). The original is not: t=1 p15 = 59 (10 fps) / 51 (20 fps) / 46 (40 fps), t=2 p0 = 102/93/89. The offset scales as exactly 1/fps, i.e. the original runs a constant ONE FRAME ahead of the pure time function while the port evaluates absolute elapsed time. Rates and total duration are identical at every fps, so this is a fixed one-frame phase, not a speed divergence, and it is the source of the 1-2 px front lag above.

STEADY STATE: after ~6.2 s all 60 pixels are 255,255,255 on both sides except pixel 0. The original keeps creeping asymptotically toward white there (p0 = 255,248,247 at t=6, 255,254,254 at t=200 and t=204), while the port freezes at 255,248,246 and never moves again (checked to t=500). Mean-channel over the long survey: orig 255/243/241 at 20 s drifting to 255/253/253 at 480 s; port pinned at 255/244/241 for the whole 500 s. One pixel, <10 counts — imperceptible, but it means the original's ramp is asymptotic while the port's terminates.
The lit wedge is asymmetric by one pixel on BOTH sides (centre sits at flat index 30, not 29.5, so pixel 0 always trails pixel 59) — the port reproduces this quirk correctly.

NOT clock-driven: byte-identical dumps on both sides at --wall-clock 1756000000 / +6 h / +12 h / +18 h. The known time-of-day engine gap is therefore irrelevant to this slug — neither side reads it, and nothing about the comparison is blocked by it.
NOT seed-driven: seed 1234 reproduces seed 1 exactly on both sides (orig t=1 centre 178,21,0; port 169,45,0 at both seeds). Fully deterministic, no RNG.

Both sides are INDEX-ONLY and resolution-independent in the same way: at --pixels 12, 60 and 300 the wedge occupies the same FRACTION of the strip at the same times (t=0.6 lit span 28.7-71.3% at 300 px vs 30-70% at 60 px), and an 8x8 grid re-render is just the 64-pixel flat ramp reshaped, symmetric about the flat-index midpoint, on both sides. No index-mapping divergence.
feedback: The single fix that closes most of the gap: the port's green channel is ~2.3x too strong through the warm phase. The original's warm ramp keeps G = 0.118*R (railing at 255,30,0, hue ~7 deg); the port keeps G = 0.267*R (railing at 255,68,0, hue ~16 deg). Scale the port's green contribution during the pre-white phase down by ~0.44 so the held plateau colour lands on 255,30,0 instead of 255,68,0. Everything else about the ramp — its speed, its expansion rate, its hold, its endpoints — is already correct.

Second colour fix: during the whitening phase the port's blue lags green too far. The original begins lifting blue once green reaches ~32/255 and keeps a G-B gap of about 27 that shrinks to 0 as it whitens; the port waits until green reaches ~64/255 and keeps a gap of about 50. Result: the original transitions red -> salmon/pink -> white, the port transitions orange -> amber/peach -> white. Start blue's rise earlier and narrow the gap to roughly half its current value.

Optional, cosmetic: the port trails the original by exactly one rendered frame (~0.05 s at 20 fps, showing up as its expansion fronts sitting 1-2 px behind). The original advances its ramp accumulator BEFORE rendering, so at frame k it shows the state for time (k+1)/fps; the port shows k/fps. Advancing the port's time by one frame delta before evaluating would make the two coincide. Note the tradeoff: the port as it stands is exactly frame-rate-invariant and the original is not, so this only matters if bit-matching the original is the goal.

Optional, near-invisible: the original's approach to full white is asymptotic and never quite finishes — pixel 0 is still climbing (255,254,254) at t=200 s and t=500 s. The port's ramp terminates and freezes pixel 0 at 255,248,246 by ~t=12 s. If the port clamps or completes its ramp at a finite time, letting it keep approaching white instead would match; the visible difference is under 10 counts on one pixel.
